title: The Citizenship Test: One Date Decides Which Version You Take
description: Two naturalization civics tests are in use at the same time. Which one you sit is decided by when USCIS received your Form N-400, and the two are not the same size.
meta_description: Two naturalization civics tests are in use at once. Which one you take depends on when USCIS received your Form N-400, and they differ in size.
main_html:
Quick answer

There are two naturalization civics tests in service right now, and nothing about you decides which one you take. One date does: when you filed Form N-400.

USCIS states it plainly: “Aliens who file Form N-400 to apply for naturalization before Oct. 20, 2025, will take the 2008 naturalization civics test. Aliens who file Form N-400 to apply for naturalization on or after Oct. 20, 2025, will take the 2025 test.”

This matters more than a version number suggests. The two tests differ in how many questions the bank holds, how many you are asked, and how many you must get right. A study set written for one will not prepare you for the other, and most study material in circulation was written for the 2008 test.

The two tests, side by side

2008 civics test2025 civics test
Who takes itApplicants who filed Form N-400 before Oct. 20, 2025Applicants who filed Form N-400 on or after Oct. 20, 2025
Size of the question bank100 questions128 questions
Questions asked at interviewUp to 1020
Correct answers needed to pass612
Point at which you fail5 answered incorrectly9 answered incorrectly
When the officer stops askingAt 6 correct or 5 incorrectAt 12 correct or 9 incorrect
Official study list100 Civics Questions and Answers128 Civics Questions and Answers

Source: USCIS, Study for the Test, uscis.gov/citizenship/find-study-materials-and-resources/study-for-the-test.

The passing threshold is proportionally the same — six of ten and twelve of twenty are both sixty per cent — but the 2025 test doubles the number of questions asked and widens the bank by twenty-eight. There is more surface area to prepare, and less room for a lucky draw.

USCIS describes the 2025 test as based on the 2020 naturalization civics test, with some modifications to the administration of the test, and published a Notice of Implementation of 2025 Naturalization Test in the Federal Register. It gives its reason for the filing-date cutoff directly: to ensure sufficient time for the public to become familiar with the revised content.

The English test is three separate things

The civics test gets the attention, but the English requirement is assessed in three parts, and only two of them look like a test.

  • Reading. You read one of three sentences aloud correctly.
  • Writing. You write one of three sentences correctly.
  • Speaking. There is no separate speaking exam. USCIS says your ability to speak and understand English is determined by the officer during the eligibility interview on Form N-400 itself.

That last one is the part applicants prepare for least. The interview is the speaking test. It starts when the officer greets you, not when a section is announced.

USCIS publishes an official writing-test vocabulary list. It is a finite list, which makes it one of the few parts of this process you can actually finish preparing for.

The answers that change under you

Some civics answers are not fixed facts. They are the names of people currently in office, and they change with elections and appointments.

USCIS is explicit about the standard: “You must answer the question with the name of the official serving at the time of your naturalization interview.” Not the official serving when you filed. Not the one printed in the study booklet you bought.

Questions to ask: confirm each of these against the USCIS Check for Test Updates page in the week before your interview, and ask the officer nothing you could have looked up.

  1. Your state’s U.S. Senators, and your U.S. Representative
  2. The President and the Vice President
  3. The political party of the President
  4. The Speaker of the House of Representatives
  5. The Chief Justice of the United States
  6. The Governor of your state

USCIS maintains that page for both test versions, and notes the cases that catch people out: residents of the District of Columbia and of U.S. territories answer that they have no U.S. Senators, and D.C. residents answer that D.C. does not have a Governor.

Common mistake: studying from a printed booklet or a video published before the last election and never checking the updates page.

What the test costs

Nothing, separately. There is no fee for the civics test or the English test. The money in a naturalization case is the Form N-400 filing fee, and that is published.

SituationFiling fee
General filing, paper$760
General filing, online$710
Documented household income not over 400% of the Federal Poverty Guidelines$380 (paper only)
Qualifying military service under INA sections 328 or 329$0
Approved fee waiver, Form I-912$0

Source: Form G-1055, the USCIS fee schedule, edition 05/29/26. USCIS notes that there is often a $50 discount when filing a form online. Note that the reduced fee is listed for paper filing only. Check the current fee schedule before you pay anything, and confirm on uscis.gov which route your filing takes.

Free study material is published by USCIS itself, including the official question lists and a study guide for the 2025 test. Anyone charging you for the question bank is selling you a government document.

Form N-400 Checklist: The Documents USCIS Asks For

Quick answer

USCIS publishes a "Checklist of Required Initial Evidence" on its own Form N-400 page. It is worth reading first, and it comes with two warnings.

USCIS says the checklist "is an optional tool to use as you prepare your form but does not replace statutory, regulatory, and form instruction requirements." The form instructions govern.

And: "Do not send original documents unless specifically requested in the form instructions or applicable regulations."

What every applicant provides

  • A copy of the Permanent Resident Card, both sides
  • Marital status documents: current marriage certificate, plus any divorce decree, annulment decree or death certificate ending a prior marriage
  • Form N-648 if a physical or developmental disability or mental impairment prevents compliance with the English or civics requirements
  • Good moral character documentation for any arrest, detention, charge, conviction or alternative sentencing programme, anywhere in the world
  • Continuous residence evidence for any trip abroad longer than six months but under a year
  • A Selective Service status information letter, where registration was required and did not happen

The translation rule catches people out. Any document in a foreign language needs a full English translation plus a certification from the translator that the translation is complete and accurate and that they are competent to translate.

Documents that depend on your basis for filing

Filing as the spouse of a US citizen adds a layer: the marriage certificate, evidence of the spouse's citizenship for the last three years, and evidence that all prior marriages for both of you were terminated.

Continuous residence evidence for the last three years applies instead of the longer period. Acceptable evidence USCIS names includes rent or mortgage statements, pay statements, bank or credit card statements showing regular transactions, car registration and insurance, passport entry and exit stamps, and IRS tax transcripts.

Applicants filing through a legal guardian, surrogate or designated representative have their own separate document set. Read the checklist section that matches your basis rather than the general one.

Questions to settle before you file

  • Which basis for filing applies to you, and what does it add?
  • Does any document need a certified English translation?
  • Are you eligible for the reduced fee or a fee waiver?
  • Is there any arrest or charge anywhere in the world that needs documenting?
  • Do you have a trip abroad over six months that needs residence evidence?

Common mistake: sending originals. USCIS asks for copies unless the instructions say otherwise.

USCIS Interview Checklist: What to Bring and What to Confirm

Quick answer

Bring the appointment notice, government photo identification, and every original of every copy you filed.

Then bring evidence of anything that has changed since you filed. That is where most interviews run into difficulty.

The official checklist is the appointment notice itself. It lists what USCIS wants from you. Start there, and treat this page as the second pass.

Fees, so nothing is outstanding on the day

From Form G-1055, edition 05/29/26.

FormFiling fee
N-400, Application for NaturalizationPaper $760 / online $710
N-400, reduced fee (household income not over 400% of the Federal Poverty Guidelines)Paper $380
N-400 with an approved fee waiver (Form I-912)$0
I-485, applicant over 14Paper $1,440 / online $1,390
I-693, Report of Immigration Medical Examination$0

The medical exam form is free to file. The exam is not, and its price is set by the civil surgeon.

Documents to assemble

  • The interview appointment notice
  • Permanent resident card and any government photo identification
  • Passports, including expired ones covering the relevant period
  • Originals of every document you submitted as a copy
  • Evidence of anything that changed: address, employment, marital status, travel, arrests
  • Tax records if the application depends on them
  • Any sealed medical envelope you have been told to bring, still sealed

Do not open a sealed civil surgeon envelope on your own initiative. There are two published exceptions, and neither is a matter of judgement.

  • Filing Form I-485 online. USCIS instructs you to open it: “If you file Form I-485 online, you must open the sealed envelope from the civil surgeon and upload the completed Form I-693 with your application package.” You then keep the original form and the envelope until USCIS decides the case, because it may ask to see them at the interview.
  • A returned, rejected package. If a lockbox rejects your filing and returns it with the envelope already opened, USCIS says you may refile using that original opened Form I-693 in its original envelope, with a copy of the rejection notice.

Outside those two cases, filing by mail, it stays sealed. Source: USCIS, Form I-693 page, uscis.gov/i-693. See the Form I-693 instructions guide for the full rule.

The medical exam validity question

If your case involves Form I-693, confirm before the interview whether the one you filed is still valid or whether a new one is expected.

Check the current guidance on the USCIS I-693 page rather than relying on what was true when you filed. This is a rule that has changed more than once.

Questions to settle beforehand

  • Is an interpreter permitted, and have you arranged one?
  • Is anything on your application now out of date?
  • Is the medical exam still valid for your case?
  • Do you need to bring anyone with you?
  • Is any fee still outstanding?

Common mistake: bringing copies where the notice asked for originals.

What to do next

  1. Find the date USCIS received your N-400. Your receipt notice carries it.
  2. Work out which test that date puts you in, using the table above.
  3. Download the matching official question list — 100 questions or 128 — from uscis.gov.
  4. Discard any study material that does not name your test version.
  5. Check the six changeable answers against the USCIS updates page shortly before your interview.
  6. If age, length of residence, or a medical condition may apply to you, read the exemptions guide before you start studying anything.

Sources used on this page: USCIS, Study for the Test; USCIS, Check for Test Updates; USCIS, Exceptions and Accommodations; Form G-1055, USCIS fee schedule, edition 05/29/26. All at uscis.gov.

Educational only. Not legal advice. USCIS policy on the naturalization test has changed recently and can change again; confirm the current rule on uscis.gov before you rely on it.
